title: How do you optimize Kafka for high throughput (batch.size, linger.ms, compression, acks, max.in.flight)?
shortTitle: How do you optimize Kafka for high throughput (batch.size, linger.ms, compression, acks, max.in.flight)?

s1_definition.profdef: High producer throughput in Kafka comes from batching more records per request, allowing a small delay to fill those batches, compressing them, and keeping several requests in flight at once. The key knobs are `batch.size` (how many bytes accumulate per partition before sending), `linger.ms` (how long to wait to fill a batch), `compression.type` (shrink the batch), `acks` (how many acknowledgements to wait for), and `max.in.flight.requests.per.connection` (how many unacknowledged requests are allowed). You tune these together, balancing throughput against latency and durability.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India sending transaction forms to the central office. Instead of one courier trip per form, the clerk waits a few seconds to collect a stack of forms into one envelope. A bigger envelope means fewer trips. If the clerk compresses the stack, the envelope is lighter. If several couriers can be on the road at once rather than one at a time, more mail moves per minute. But waiting too long to fill the envelope delays each form, so there is a balance between speed-per-form and total mail moved.
s1_definition.oneliner: Bigger batches plus a little linger plus compression plus several in-flight requests maximize throughput, while acks and in-flight settings keep you safe from loss and reordering.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** High producer throughput in Kafka comes from batching more records per request, allowing a small delay to fill those batches, compressing them, and keeping several requests in flight at once. The key knobs are `batch.size` (how many bytes accumulate per partition before sending), `linger.ms` (how long to wait to fill a batch), `compression.type` (shrink the batch), `acks` (how many acknowledgements to wait for), and `max.in.flight.requests.per.connection` (how many unacknowledged requests are allowed). You tune these together, balancing throughput against latency and durability.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India sending transaction forms to the central office. Instead of one courier trip per form, the clerk waits a few seconds to collect a stack of forms into one envelope. A bigger envelope means fewer trips. If the clerk compresses the stack, the envelope is lighter. If several couriers can be on the road at once rather than one at a time, more mail moves per minute. But waiting too long to fill the envelope delays each form, so there is a balance between speed-per-form and total mail moved.

**One line to remember:** Bigger batches plus a little linger plus compression plus several in-flight requests maximize throughput, while acks and in-flight settings keep you safe from loss and reordering.

sections.s2_technical:
The `batch.size` setting, defaulting to 16384 bytes, controls how many bytes the producer accumulates per partition before sending a batch. Larger batches mean fewer, bigger requests, which is more efficient. You might set `props.put("batch.size", 65536)` for sixty-four kilobyte batches in a high-volume transaction feed. The batch is sent when it fills up or when the linger time elapses, whichever comes first.

The `linger.ms` setting, defaulting to zero, is how long the producer waits to let a batch fill before sending it. With the default of zero, the producer sends as soon as it can, which gives low latency but small batches. Setting `props.put("linger.ms", 10)` tells the producer to wait up to ten milliseconds, which dramatically improves batching under load because many records arrive in that window. The cost is up to ten milliseconds of added latency per record.

The `compression.type` setting shrinks the batch before it goes over the network. Because Kafka compresses the whole batch, a larger batch compresses better, so `linger.ms` and compression reinforce each other. For throughput, `props.put("compression.type", "lz4")` or `zstd` is common because they compress well with low CPU cost. The broker stores the compressed batch and the consumer decompresses it, saving network and disk end to end.

The `acks` setting trades durability against throughput. `acks=0` is fastest but can silently lose data, `acks=1` waits for the leader only, and `acks=all` waits for all in-sync replicas. In banking you keep `props.put("acks", "all")` for correctness and squeeze throughput from batching and compression instead of weakening durability.

The `max.in.flight.requests.per.connection` setting, defaulting to five, controls how many unacknowledged batches can be in flight on one connection. Higher values improve throughput because the producer does not wait for each batch to be acknowledged before sending the next. A crucial nuance is that with the idempotent producer enabled, Kafka preserves ordering even with up to five in-flight requests, so you get both high throughput and no reordering. Without idempotence, more than one in-flight request risks reordering on retry.

A senior-level point is that these settings interact. A big `batch.size` is useless without `linger.ms` because under light load the batch never fills and ships half-empty. Compression amplifies the benefit of larger batches. And you should also raise `buffer.memory` if the producer accumulates many batches, otherwise `send()` blocks or throws when the buffer is full. Finally, more partitions allow more parallelism on both producer and consumer side, so topic design is part of throughput tuning too.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India runs an end-of-day batch that publishes millions of transaction events to a Kafka topic for the analytics and fraud systems. During peak the naive producer, sending one record at a time, cannot keep up and the batch job runs for hours.

Problem 1 — the producer sends every transaction as its own tiny request, so most of the time is spent on request overhead rather than moving data. This is exactly what `batch.size` and `linger.ms` solve: the producer collects many transactions into one larger request.

Problem 2 — the batches are large JSON and saturate the network. This is exactly what `compression.type` solves: compressing the batch shrinks it before it travels.

Problem 3 — the producer waits for each batch to be acknowledged before sending the next, wasting the round-trip time. This is exactly what `max.in.flight.requests.per.connection` plus idempotence solves: several batches travel at once while ordering is still guaranteed.

The code will show a throughput-tuned producer publishing a burst of transaction events for Rajesh and Priya, and log the configured knobs and the achieved rate.

```yaml
# application.yml
spring:
  kafka:
    bootstrap-servers: broker1:9092
    producer:
      acks: all
      properties:
        enable.idempotence: true
        batch.size: 65536                 # 64 KB batches
        linger.ms: 10                     # wait up to 10 ms to fill a batch
        compression.type: lz4             # fast compression, low CPU
        max.in.flight.requests.per.connection: 5
        buffer.memory: 67108864           # 64 MB send buffer
```

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: one million transaction events, alternating between Rajesh (SAV2001) and Priya (CUR3001).

Step 1 — each `send()` call does not immediately hit the network. The record is appended to an in-memory batch for its partition. Because the key is the account, Rajesh's events accumulate in one partition's batch and Priya's in another.

Step 2 — a batch is sent when it reaches sixty-four kilobytes or when ten milliseconds of linger time elapse. Under a heavy burst, batches fill to full size almost instantly, so each request carries hundreds of events instead of one.

Step 3 — before sending, the producer compresses the batch with lz4, shrinking the JSON significantly, so the network carries far fewer bytes.

Step 4 — up to five batches are in flight per connection at once. Because idempotence is enabled, Kafka assigns sequence numbers so even with five in-flight requests and retries, the broker writes them in order and drops duplicates.

Step 5 — with `acks=all`, each batch is acknowledged only after the in-sync replicas store it, so durability is preserved. After `flush()`, the demo logs the total time and the achieved events per second.

```
2026-10-24 21:40:12 [INFO] Published 1,000,000 events in 4,120 ms (242718 events/sec)
```

```
  App loop: send 1,000,000 TxnEvents (Rajesh / Priya)
    │  each send() appends to an in-memory batch (NOT network yet)
    ▼
  Producer RecordAccumulator
    ├─ partition 0 batch (SAV2001 events)  ──┐
    ├─ partition 1 batch (CUR3001 events)  ──┤  fill to batch.size (64 KB)
    │                                         │  OR linger.ms (10 ms) elapses
    ▼                                         ▼
  Compress batch (lz4)  → much smaller bytes
    │
    │ up to 5 in-flight requests per connection
    │ idempotence → sequence numbers keep order, drop dups
    ▼
  Broker leader → replicate to ISR → acks=all → ACK
    │
    ▼
  Topic transactions (events stored compressed on disk)
    │
    ▼
  Consumers fetch & decompress → analytics / fraud
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
To optimize Kafka for high throughput I tune five knobs together. The batch size controls how many bytes accumulate per partition before a request is sent, and a larger batch means fewer, more efficient requests. The linger time tells the producer to wait a few milliseconds so batches actually fill up under load, which is essential because a large batch size does nothing if the batch always ships half empty.

Compression shrinks the batch before it travels, and because Kafka compresses the whole batch, a larger batch compresses even better, so linger and compression reinforce each other. For throughput I usually pick a fast codec like lz4 or zstd that compresses well with low CPU cost, and the broker stores and ships the compressed batch while the consumer decompresses it.

The acknowledgement setting trades durability against speed, but in banking I never weaken it. I keep all-acknowledgements and instead get throughput from batching and compression. The in-flight requests setting lets several batches travel at once instead of waiting for each one to be acknowledged, and crucially, with the idempotent producer enabled, ordering is still guaranteed up to five in-flight requests, so I get both high throughput and no reordering.

In my National Bank of India project, the end-of-day job published millions of transaction events for the analytics and fraud systems. The naive one-record-at-a-time producer could not keep up, but after setting sixty-four kilobyte batches, a ten millisecond linger, lz4 compression, and five in-flight requests with idempotence, throughput jumped by an order of magnitude while durability stayed at all-acknowledgements. We also added partitions so both producers and consumers could work in parallel.
